children: US Midterms Betting Odds: Polymarket’s market for Which party will win the Senate in 2026? showed Democrats at 66% and Republicans at 35% as of September 23, 2026, at 7:30 AM UTC. That is a full reversal from earlier snapshots in the campaign that had Republicans as the favorite, and it matters because prediction markets put real money behind political forecasts in a way polls cannot.

Here is the tension worth sitting with: a 65.5% price is a trader-implied probability, not a poll result, and not a guarantee of what happens on November 3, 2026. It reflects how people with capital at stake are currently weighing the odds, and those odds can move again before a single vote is counted. children: US Midterms Betting Odds: From GOP Favorite to Democratic Lead

Republicans currently hold a 53–47 majority in the Senate, and 22 of the chamber’s 35 seats are up for election in 2026, according to the primary market data behind Polymarket’s Senate-control event. That is a wide swath of the map in play, and it is the raw seat math that traders are pricing against.

The same market data points to Democratic candidates leading or competitive in several Republican-held battlegrounds, including Alaska, Iowa, Maine, Ohio, and Texas. Polymarket’s event page also cites a national generic-ballot advantage for Democrats of roughly eight points, along with elevated “wrong track” sentiment among voters heading into the fall.

Those are the inputs behind the 65.5% Democratic price. The figure is a snapshot rather than a fixed number pinned to a single moment. For a wider view of how Democratic pricing has shifted across Polymarket’s 2026 midterm lineup,

Why the Map Moved: Battlegrounds, Ballot and Backlash
The structural story is straightforward once you separate the markets. Polymarket doesn’t run one midterm market – it runs several, and they measure different things.

The Senate-control market is distinct from the “Balance of Power: 2026 Midterms” event, which prices a full Democratic sweep of both chambers separately from a Senate-control-only scenario. Conflating the two overstates or understates either number, so here’s how the related markets stacked up on Polymarket’s predictions page, alongside a House-control figure reported by Yahoo Finance and Benzinga on September 21:

Notice the gap: Democrats are priced far more heavily to win the House than the Senate. That’s the Senate map talking – a chamber where individual state races in Alaska, Iowa, Maine, Ohio and Texas can swing control regardless of the national mood. Yahoo Finance and Benzinga reported on September 21 that Polymarket’s Senate market showed Democrats at roughly 60% against 42% for Republicans just two days before the event page’s 66% reading, and that the broader sweep market had traded above $12 million in volume.
